title: Batch waitstate deconv and stage-slices
content:
Executive summary:

We ran a trace-driven decomposition to isolate where per-request latency is accumulating under high concurrent throughput when the batcher is enabled. Goal: understand p95/p99 regressions observed in production for the last three deploys (notably a 12-18% p99 increase for 512-token requests). This note captures the aggregation approach, representative waterfall slices, hypotheses that survived initial checks, and concrete experiments to validate fixes.

What we looked at:
- 72k anonymized traces sampled across 10 clusters (eu-west/us-west) over a 48h window (2025-02-09 — 2025-02-10). Sampling prioritized heavy requests: seqlen >= 256 and responses >= 128 tokens.
- Instrumentation: end-to-end trace with stage timers: ingress-network, auth+quota, routing, prefetch/kvcache (lookup), batcher-wait, cuda-kernel (attn/ff), kvcache-write, decode-loop, response-escape/egress.
- We augmented traces with batch metadata: batch_size_at_dispatch, batch_age_ms, batch_client_qps_bucket.

Headline numbers (aggregate):
- All requests (sample window): p50=78ms, p95=318ms, p99=672ms.
- Sliced by seqlen: 64 tokens p99=220ms; 256 tokens p99=520ms; 512 tokens p99=860ms.
- For requests with batch_size>=8 at dispatch: median batch_age_ms=34ms, p95 batch_age_ms=156ms.

Per-stage breakdown (median and p95 for 512-token slice):
- ingress-network: median 8ms, p95 22ms
- auth+quota: median 3ms, p95 9ms
- routing: median 6ms, p95 18ms
- prefetch/kvcache lookup: median 4ms (hit), p95 72ms (miss+remote-read)
- batcher-wait: median 34ms, p95 210ms
- cuda-kernel compute (attention+FF): median 110ms, p95 290ms
- kvcache-write: median 6ms, p95 40ms
- decode-loop + streamer: median 22ms, p95 62ms
- egress: median 3ms, p95 9ms

Observations and key signals:
1) Batcher-wait dominant at p95/p99 for mid-to-high concurrency. When request inter-arrival variance is high, batcher holds micro-batches open waiting for slow stragglers. p95 batch_age correlates with p99 overall latency (Pearson r=0.71).
2) kvcache lookup/miss variance creates stragglers. Misses that trigger remote read (from backing store) add 40–120ms on p95 tails. These often coincide with batcher-wait spikes because the request that missed tends to be the final member of a batch.
3) Compute is predictable but non-negligible. On GPUs we observed kernel p99 variations when NV-links are saturated in busy nodes (manifested as slower all-reduce for some attention kernels). This is a second-order effect compared to batching and cache misses.
4) A small fraction (~3%) of traces show long routing/egress delays (>200ms) attributable to overloaded edge proxies; these are outside serving runtime scope but inflate global p99. Filtering these reduces p99 by ~6% for 512 slice.

Representative trace archetypes (examples):
- Archetype A: Batch-slow due to straggler kv-miss
  - batch_size_at_dispatch: 8
  - batch_age_ms: 198 (p99)
  - timeline: ingress(9) → kv-lookup(miss, remote-read 74) → batch-wait accumulated (waiting for remaining 7, many already compute-ready) → dispatch → compute(118) → decode(24) → write-kv(12) → egress(4)
  - end-to-end: 551ms
  - root cause: kvcache miss that delayed one request and held batch open; others incur wait.

- Archetype B: High batch_age from bursty arrivals
  - batch_size_at_dispatch: 12
  - batch_age_ms: 312
  - timeline: multiple small arrivals across 300ms window; no heavy kv-misses, but batcher policy leaves window open to reach min_batch_size.
  - end-to-end: 780ms (512 slice)
  - root cause: conservative batcher timeout/min_batch thresholds creating tail latency during bursty arrivals.

- Archetype C: Compute tail from NV-link congestion
  - batch_size_at_dispatch: 16
  - batch_age_ms: 42
  - timeline: normal prefetch hits → dispatch → compute(450ms p99 on this node) → decode(28)
  - end-to-end: 610ms
  - root cause: node-level interconnect saturation, intermittent.

Hypotheses tested so far and outcome:
- H1: Reduce batcher timeout reduces p99. Quick A/B with timeout 25ms -> 40ms slices on one pool: p95 improved 9%, p99 improved 12% for 256/512 slices, but throughput at peak decreased 6% and cost increased due to more small batches. Tradeoff looks real.
- H2: Pre-warming kvcache for hot-prefixes will reduce tail. Simulation using held-hot-prefix at 1% higher hit-rate predicted p99 drop of ~7% for heavy seqlen flows. Need production experiment.
- H3: Prioritize requests with remote-dependency early to avoid being last in a batch. Implemented a heuristic in local test (assign "early-dispatch" flag when estimated remote-read expected > 30ms). This lowered batch_age_ms p95 by ~18% in tests but introduced unfair latency for small quick requests — needs fairness constraints.

Suggested remediation roadmap (short → medium → long):
- Short term (1-2 sprints):
  1) Canary a reduced batcher timeout with auto-fallback when throughput drops below threshold (configurable per-queue). Owner: Aisha. JIRA: JIRA-SRV-7902.
  2) Add trace-level kvcache-miss tagging to the metrics (already instrumented but not surfaced). Create dashboard for "batch-final-member remote-read" slices. Owner: Marcus.

- Medium term (2-6 sprints):
  1) Implement request-prioritization heuristic: requests likely to block on I/O get earlier dispatch. Must couple with fairness policy to avoid penalizing fast requests. Rollout as config flag. Owner: Ravi.
  2) Explore compact prefetch for trending prefixes: background prefetcher for top-k prefixes per tenant. Measure cost vs p99 wins.

- Long term (quarter):
  1) Adaptive batcher: dynamically tune timeouts and min-batch-size by observing per-route inter-arrival distribution. This would require online distribution estimation and quick reconfiguration.
  2) Kernel-level improvements for interconnect variance: collaborate with infra to surface NVLink/PCIe counters per-GPU for better scheduling.

Open questions and experiments to run:
- How much of the p99 is reducible if we only address kvcache remote reads? Run a targeted experiment: pin hot workload with pre-warmed cache and measure p99 delta.
- Can we implement a per-request latency SLO budget that the batcher uses to decide to dispatch early vs wait for batch efficiency? Model-driven feasibility required.
- Fairness rules for early dispatch: how to avoid serializing many small requests at cost of bulk clients? Need microbench sims.

Immediate action items (this week):
- [ ] Dashboard to expose batch_age_ms distribution by route and seqlen. (Marcus)
- [ ] Canary reduced timeout on a low-cost pool, monitor throughput drop and p99. (Aisha)
- [ ] Instrument a trace tag for "kv-remote-read" and surface in trace explorer. (Ravi)

Notes / stray observations:
- Some tenants on Dedicated pools show lower p99 despite similar QPS because their batch_size_at_dispatch is smaller (single-tenant effect). Suggests multi-tenancy mixing is amplifying batcher tail in shared pools.
- For low-latency routes (target p95 < 80ms) we should consider min_batch_size=1 by default.

Appendix: quick methodology notes
- Aggregation: per-request total latency = sum(stage durations). We use trace-level sampling (1:50 for normal, 1:5 for suspect routes) and adjusted weights when generating percentiles to correct sampling bias.
- Batcher instrumentation capture points: arrival_time, eligibility_time, dispatch_time, kernel_start, kernel_end, decode_end, egress_sent. Batch_age_ms=dispatch_time-eligibility_time. This is the most useful derived metric.
- When filtering external-edge-inflated traces, we used edge-proxy header "x-edge-latency" > 150ms to exclude.

If you want the raw aggregated trace dumps (CSV with per-trace slices) I uploaded them to the confluence page linked above (trace-sample-2025-02). Next meeting: Tuesday 14:00 engineering sync — I will present the canary plan and simulation results.

-- Marcus
